4.0.0.en: After this: that is, after the previous talk and vision about the seven churches.

4.0.1.en: A door was opened in heaven: spiritually it means the opening of the spirit to see new spiritual things that were closed to all men.

4.0.2.en: This verse reminds us of the opening of heaven before Stephen at the time of his martyrdom (Acts 7:56) and the ladder that Jacob saw, which joined heaven and earth; both Stephen and Jacob saw something of heaven while on earth, but in John's vision he will see heaven from within heaven, and he will also see, while in heaven, successive events that happen on earth.

4.0.3.en: Since the Church represents heaven on earth, the rite of the Church has continued to forbid the closing of her doors, as a sign that for whoever wants heaven its door is always open, and this rite remained in force and was set aside only by conditions of security.

4.0.4.en: The first voice: it is the same voice of Christ (ch. 1:10).

4.0.5.en: Come up hither: that is, that John, and after him the whole Church, may see something of the glory of heaven, and this is what the Master added by saying "and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter," and the basic purpose of God's declaring to us some scenes of the glory of heaven is to encourage us to be constantly attached to it and to look toward it, so that nothing may distract us from it and we lose our place in it.

4.0.6.en: After the vision of the seven letters, Christ spoke to John and declared to him a new vision, as he entered through an open door into heaven to see what would happen after the vision of the seven churches.

4.1.0.en: Immediately I was in the spirit: St. John declared before that he was in the Spirit (ch. 1:10), and now he declares here that he became in the Spirit, meaning that God gave him a new spiritual sense with his transfer to heaven, a sense that fits the new scene he was about to see, and so also every person who listens to the voice of the Master, as John heard, God gives him a distinctive spiritual feeling that is hard for a person to describe to others.

4.1.1.en: One sat on the throne: human language with all its vocabulary did not help St. John to describe the divine Self, but what God permitted him to see was One sitting on a throne, and this scene accords with our describing heaven as the kingdom of God (that is, His kingdom) and also points to the absolute authority of the One who sits on this throne.

4.1.2.en: St. John will use the expression "him that sat on the throne" often in the coming chapters.

4.2.0.en: As for the appearance of this One who sat on the throne, He was to look upon like a jasper stone, white and transparent, as an expression of God's simplicity and purity, and likewise the sardine stone is red like fire, so it signifies the justice of God, and He is steadfast in His covenants with men, as the memorial of the covenant of the rainbow (Gen 9:13) which He gave to Noah after the Flood and to all mankind, that He would not drown them again with a flood, while the green emerald points to God being the source of all life and growth. And all these things (the jasper, the sardine stone and the rainbow) point to the splendor of the glory of God.

4.3.0.en: The four and twenty seats: John saw twenty-four thrones for heavenly beings around the throne of the One who sits, that is, God made them partners in His council, which is a very special kind of honor.

4.3.1.en: Four and twenty elders: who are they: we prefer to use the expression heavenly beings, an expression that includes their being distinguished angels or something greater than the angels, as many of the Fathers said. Elders: the Greek origin of this word means priests, so the correct translation of it is priests and not elders.

4.3.2.en: Four and twenty: this number signifies the completeness of the Church in her two covenants before God (the twelve tribes of the Old Testament and the twelve apostles of the New Testament), and the twenty-four priests represent the priesthood standing before God, which intercedes for the believers and conveys their prayers to God (Rev 5:8), and the white garments they wear represent their purity (like the tunic of the priest and the deacon), while the crowns of gold signify the glory and honor of this exalted rank before God, since He made them like kings, and the Coptic people in general are distinguished by their reverence and respect for the priesthood and its ranks because of the loftiness of its work, since it is the sacrament that completes all the sacraments of the Church, and it has its honor before God.

4.3.3.en: Note: the Church keeps the feast of the twenty-four priests on the 24th of Hathor, and asks for their intercession and remembers them in her Midnight Praise.

4.4.0.en: Lightnings and thunderings and voices: these phenomena are connected with the divine presence and point to it, since they were repeated on Mount Sinai at the giving of the Law (Ex 19:16), and all of them make us feel awe and trembling when standing before God, and remembering such things helps a person to resist evil thoughts (wandering of mind) at the time of prayer.

4.4.1.en: Seven lamps of fire burning: a reference to the Holy Spirit, fiery and giving light, for the Apostle goes on to say "which are the seven Spirits of God"; see (ch. 1:12); it also points to His work in the seven sacraments of the Church. It can also be said that the "lightnings" represent God's gentle, shining promises, while the thunderings represent His awesome warnings, and the voices express His speech and His will declared in creation.

4.5.0.en: A sea of glass like unto crystal: in the Old Testament and in Solomon's temple there was "a molten sea" (1 Kgs 7:23) and it was for purification.. and now we are before a sea of crystal glass that signifies Baptism in its purity and cleanness, and this sea is before God because no one will see God unless he passes through this Baptism (Jn 3:5). Four beasts full of eyes: what is meant by four beasts is that they are four living beings, and all the Fathers agreed in their interpretations that they are the orders of angels known as the Seraphim and Cherubim, and to complete the explanation about them we will clarify that in the interpretation of verses (7-9).

4.5.1.en: How beautiful, wonderful and awesome is the scene of heaven that lifts us and raises us to contemplate the glory of God and His throne, so that we long for constant meeting with Him... I beseech You, my God, grant us a share in seeing You as John saw You, and give us the good will to complete our striving in peace.

4.6.s.en: (2) The description of the four beasts and their work

4.6.0.en: 1- Full of eyes: that is, distinguished by God's universal knowledge and many other things that God reveals to them, and these eyes within (v. 8) are also a proof of strong inner knowledge.

4.7.0.en: 2- Their visible forms: like a lion... like a calf... a face as a man... like a flying eagle.

4.7.1.en: (a) The tradition of the Church from of old has taken the forms of these angelic beings as symbols of the four Gospels: the lion points to the Gospel of St. Mark because it begins with a crying voice, and the lion has been linked with the image of St. Mark; the likeness of the calf points to the Gospel of St. Luke because he spoke most about the sacrifices; the face of a man points to St. Matthew because he begins by mentioning the human genealogy of Christ; and the likeness of the eagle points to the Gospel of St. John because he soars in the theological matters and spoke of them much.

4.7.2.en: (b) Because these creatures are angelic, their forms also indicate their work and their standing.

4.7.3.en: The lion: a symbol of the strength and power of the angels.

4.7.4.en: The calf: patience in carrying out difficult tasks.

4.7.5.en: The man: a proof of intellectual perception and discernment.

4.7.6.en: The eagle: speed, far-sightedness and loftiness of height.

4.7.7.en: (c) We can also say that they represent the completeness of creation before God, considering that man is the most important of the rational beings, the lion the noblest of the beasts of prey, the calf represents the tame and self-giving animals, and the eagle is the strongest in the kingdom of birds, so that creation of all kinds stands before God at all times offering Him praise and worship; the four beasts intercede for all creatures.

4.8.0.en: 3- Six wings: the wings point to the swift movement of the angels in carrying out the will of God, and they also signify the awe of the sight of God and the glory of His honor, for they fly with two wings, and in reverence and modesty cover their feet with two wings, and in humility veil their faces with two wings (Isa 6:2), and this is what we also remember of them in the prayer of the Gregorian Liturgy.

4.9.0.en: Their work: it can be said that their most important and perhaps only work is offering "glory and honour and thanks" to God, declaring with their voices the hymn of sanctification "Holy, holy, holy," which is the same hymn that Isaiah saw in his vision (Isa 6), and which the Church took and added to all her prayers and hymns (the prayer of the Agpeya and the Divine Liturgy). We have nothing better than to pray to God as the angels praise Him, glorify Him and utter His name.

4.9.1.en: Their prayer also includes praising God in His attributes: He is Almighty (the Sustainer of all and the Creator of things out of nothing), and He is also the eternal, the One who is, and the everlasting, whose kingdom has no end.

4.9.2.en: 5- The Church keeps the feast of the four incorporeal beasts and asks for their intercession, in acknowledgment of their standing and the loftiness of their work, on the 8th of Hathor.

4.9.3.en: My beloved sister, if the angels, who have spiritual bodies of light, cover themselves with their wings before God out of modesty and sanctification of His honor and awe, should we not learn, and teach our children from childhood, the virtue of modesty in our clothing, and likewise covering the head and reverence during the times of prayer?! How sweet it is to stand with awe and reverence before God.

4.10.s.en: (3) The hymn of the twenty-four priests

4.10.0.en: When Isaiah heard the angels chanting "Holy.. holy.. holy," the posts of the door of the temple and its foundations shook and he was terrified and cried out, "Woe is me.. for I am a man of unclean lips" (Isa 6:3-5), and here we are before an exactly similar scene.. so when the four incorporeal beasts uttered the name of the holy God, what happened?!!

4.10.1.en: Fall down... and worship: the twenty-four priests could not bear the cry of the name of the holy God, so they immediately prostrated themselves in reverence, submission and contrition before the declaration of the glory of God.

4.10.2.en: Cast their crowns: since their crowns were a kind of honor that God gave them, they return it to Him, as though saying that You alone are the possessor of honor.

4.10.3.en: And notice, beloved, that in the rite of the liturgy of our Church the bishop enters the church with the crown of his priesthood, but at the reading of the Gospel, and even before it, at the hymn of Agios, the high priest removes his head covering, as though imitating this heavenly scene and declaring that there is no honor except to the one God who sits on His throne... and he completes the whole prayer of the Liturgy without putting the crown on again.

4.11.0.en: Here the twenty-four priests offer a hymn to the Lord God in which they declare that He alone is worthy of glory and honor, because He is Almighty and the Owner of all creation and its Maker by His word and will... and this praise includes us human beings, for we are God's creation and the work of His hands... that is, we are remembered before God in the hymn of the heavenly ones.

4.11.1.en: Do you feel this, beloved... and do you share with the heavenly ones in the divine praise?

4.11.2.en: The prayers of the Church's Midnight Praise are among the sweetest prayers that lift the heart to God, so have you enjoyed them? May you share in them with the Church, so that you may be with the heavenly ones in their high spiritual feelings.

4.11.3.en: The sealed book and the hymn of the Lamb

5.0.0.en: And I saw: that is, a new scene and sight which St. John adds to the scene in the previous chapter.

5.0.1.en: In the right hand of him that sat: the right hand signifies honor, and the book here is the Holy Bible, and the indication that it is in the right hand means the lofty standing of the word of God and the duty of reading it and doing its commandments. Within and on the backside: books were written on one side and then rolled up in the form of a cylinder, but his saying that it was written within and on the backside means:

5.0.2.en: First: the abundance of what is written and its richness, on the one hand.

5.0.3.en: Second: that there are apparent meanings and others deep and hidden in the word of God.

5.0.4.en: Sealed with seven seals: that is, this book is rolled up and closed upon itself and has upon it seven seals that signify...

5.0.5.en: 1- The firmness of its closing, and that God is the keeper of His word.

5.0.6.en: 2- The seals also signify God's covenants with men, since all the ancient treaties were not reckoned valid unless they were sealed with the seals of the king.

5.0.7.en: 3- They also signify the hidden and symbolic meanings, which need Christ, who alone is able to open them, and His Holy Spirit declares their mysteries to all men.

5.0.8.en: 4- It can also be said that they are the seven sacraments of the Church which God offered us in His holy book. This new scene in heaven which John saw is the presence of a great book, that is, at the right hand of God on His throne, and sealed with seven seals.

5.1.0.en: A strong angel: that is, strong in his voice to convey his message to all the inhabitants of heaven and earth. Who is worthy...: that is, of the honor of this book, is there anyone of all God's creation who is worthy to open its seals and disclose its mysteries?!! And this exclamatory question is considered an introduction to the answer in (v. 3).

5.2.0.en: No one of God's creation was able, because all feel their unworthiness, and this feeling did not enable them to look upon the book and its seals...

5.2.1.en: Heaven... earth... under the earth: an expression St. John used to declare the inability of anyone of God's creation, visible and invisible, men or angels or demons (under the earth), to approach this book.

5.3.0.en: St. John wept while in the Spirit after he saw the inability of all to approach the book. And this weeping means his deep sorrow at his inability to know the content of this book and his despair of anyone's ability to open it, and consequently that there was no one to save man and lift from him the judgments of God and restore his happiness to him.

5.4.0.en: God's consolation came quickly to St. John, for the tender God never delays answering a petition offered with the tears of His beloved children...

5.4.1.en: One of the elders: that is, one of the twenty-four priests near the throne, and his answer came to John to reassure him, so he commanded him: first not to weep, that is, not to grieve but to rejoice; second, he presented the Person who alone can open the book and declare its true mysteries. As for the attributes which the priest (elder) declared here, they are:

5.4.2.en: a- The Lion.. of the tribe of Juda.. of course what is meant here is the Lord Christ, for in Him the prophecy of Jacob was fulfilled (Gen 49:9), and the lion is a reference to the strength of the Lord Christ, His victory and His kingship.

5.4.3.en: b- The Root of David: that is, the originator of David and his Creator (Rom 15:12), and Christ Himself called Himself by the same title in (ch. 22:16) when He said "I am the root and the offspring of David," that is, his Creator and born of his seed according to the flesh.

5.4.4.en: The summary: no one can open the book and its seven seals except its Owner, who is Christ, to whom be glory.

5.4.5.en: Christ alone is able to save you from all your sins, so hold fast to His holy name and repeat it in all your tribulations and be nourished by His Body and Blood, and the demons will fear you.

5.5.s.en: (2) Second: the hymn of the Lamb

5.5.0.en: In the midst of the throne and of the four beasts.. and in the midst of the elders.. it is the same scene explained in detail in a Lamb as it had been slain, standing: the talk here is about the Lord Christ who rose from the dead, and in the midst of the throne means His atoning mediation between God the Father and all men, while the expression as it had been slain means that although He redeemed us and rose from the dead victorious, He bears the mark of His love and His redemption of us as a living and continual sacrifice, offering Himself to us in every Divine Liturgy so that we may enjoy union with Him and abiding in Him.

5.5.1.en: Seven horns: the horn signifies strength, and seven horns means the completeness of His strength.

5.5.2.en: Seven eyes: that is, the completeness of knowledge and penetrating insight, and St. John continues his words and says the seven Spirits of God, that is, that the completeness of His knowledge is itself His Holy Spirit who searches all things (1 Cor 2:10) and who is sent from the Son (Jn 15:26) into all the earth to complete and continue the work of God in His creation for its salvation.

5.6.0.en: So the Lamb, the sacrifice (the Son), came with all His authority and took the book out of the hand of His Father (the One who sat); and before His divinity and the power of His authority all the heavenly creation fell down in reverence to Him, as it had submitted and fallen down before the Father earlier (ch. 4:10). Harps: musical instruments used for praise in Jewish worship.

5.6.1.en: Vials: the vial is the censer set aside for burning incense.

5.6.2.en: The meaning is that the constant work of the heavenly creation before God is praise (harps) and prayer (incense), as David says, "Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense" (Ps 141:2). The prayers of saints: that is, the incense (the prayers) offered before God is not only the prayers of the heavenly creation but also the prayers of the saintly children of God, raised from all the earth, mixed with and accompanied by the prayers and intercessions of the heavenly ones before His glory, and for this reason the Church teaches us that when we conclude our prayers before God we attach to them the intercessions and petitions of the saints who always stand before God.

5.7.0.en: As for the praise they were offering, "St. John" described it as a new song.

5.7.1.en: "New" because he had not heard the like of it before among the hymns they were accustomed to pray with.

5.7.2.en: "New" because its subject was the redemption of Christ offered on the Cross and meditation on His being slain for us. "New" because the feeling of praise, although its words are repeated, is new in its feelings and taste, as though we praise every day for the first time.

5.7.3.en: "Hast redeemed us": the redemption that Christ offered was for men only, for Christ was not crucified to redeem the angelic heavenly creation; but their praising with the word "redeemed us" means that they pray and praise on behalf of the tongue of all who accepted the redemption of Christ, and this confirms the faith of the Orthodox Church in the connection of the Church of heaven with her spiritual creatures to the striving Church of God on earth, and for this reason, as we said before, we ask for their intercession and their prayers for us.

5.7.4.en: Out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation: that is, the redemption was offered in Christ to all peoples of every race and is no longer limited to one specific people.

5.7.5.en: The twenty-four priests declared their joy in Christ the Redeemer, so they sang a new song in which they declared their faith in His salvation offered to all mankind, which He accomplished on the Cross, and gave everyone who believes in Him a new life in Him.

5.8.1.en: Besides the previous interpretation of the same verse in the first chapter, it can also be said that the heavenly creation, while praising Christ its Redeemer, with our tongues also, offers Him thanks for His grace overflowing upon us, since we have become united with Him in His mystical Body (He made of us spiritual kings after His image and likeness), and just as the earth is under the feet of its king, so also it has become under our feet with all its enticements, and the death of Christ made the priests of the New Testament not offer animal sacrifices like the priests of the Old Testament but the loftiest sacrifice, which is the sacrifice of the Body and Blood of Christ which He offered on the Cross, and which they offer every day on the altar of the New Testament.

5.9.0.en: Continuing the description of the same heavenly scene, "St. John" adds that he also saw, beyond what came before, numbers of angels that cannot be counted, which he expressed as ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands. Thousands of thousands: the million or the billion was not known in counting or numbering anciently, and for this reason the expression thousands of thousands does not mean a few thousands but means thousands upon thousands, that is, the angels were numbered in the millions. And this accords of course with the expression "ten thousand times ten thousand," and the myriad is ten thousand, and what is meant is the large and vast numbers of angels who sing around the throne.

5.10.0.en: As for the subject of the praise, it was offering glorification, thanks and acknowledgment to the Lord Christ (the slain Lamb) for the sake of His redemption of us, and this hymn included 7 attributes to indicate the completeness of the attributes of the Master.

5.10.1.en: Worthy... to receive: that is, You are worthy that these attributes be ascribed to You because they are from You and You are their source. And the attributes with which Christ was described all relate to His divinity and His equality with the Father, since these attributes are also what was uttered in the hymn offered to the Father (see ch. 4:11). In summary, you, O slain Lamb (Christ the Redeemer), are: (1) The God Almighty, so we fear nothing while You are with us.

5.10.2.en: (2) Rich in Your grace, which we touch every day in our lives.

5.10.3.en: (3) You are the fullness of wisdom, for You are the Word of the Father.

5.10.4.en: (4) Yours is the strength, for by His strength He saves us from all our sins.

5.10.5.en: (5) Yours is the glory, for it is complete in His divine greatness.

5.10.6.en: (6) Honor and blessing, for He is the source of every blessing in the world and His children enjoy it in all their circumstances, and He is honored in the eyes of all the heavenly and the earthly, and nothing has honor except through Him.

5.11.0.en: This verse came as an affirmation and continuation of the previous one, but it brought out two new things:

5.11.1.en: Every creature which is in heaven and on the earth: that is, the praise was not limited to the heavenly creation but the earthly children of God also took part in it, as well as all beings (such as the fishes) and the invisible creation (under the earth). The second addition is the affirmation of the equality of the Father with the Son, since the Father and the Son (the One who sits and the Lamb) share, in the same measure, in the same words of glorification offered by all creation.

5.12.1.en: And when the hymn was offered by all the heavenly and earthly creation, those who represent it before the throne (the four beasts) answered, acknowledging and affirming all that was in it, and declaring that by their confirming reply "Amen," while the twenty-four priests did not speak but expressed the awe, honor and glory of the Lamb and of the One who sits on the throne by their prostrating and pouring themselves out before the two of them, with all the contrition and reverence that befits this awesome and wonderful scene of the Lord God.

5.12.2.en: Oh, my soul.. all creatures.. even the fishes and the mountains, indeed every breath praises the name of the Lord and glorifies Him.. so where are you in all this.. and how do you deprive yourself of sharing with the heavenly ones in praising the name of the holy Lord... begin, even with a little, and if you do not know how, why do you not strive at least by going to the church to praise and glorify the name of God?... and we now live in plenty and all the means have become available... I beseech you, my soul, not to lag behind from the beauty of this heavenly scene... for whoever praises on earth becomes numbered with the angels of heaven. Come, rise up, and do something.

5.12.3.en: The opening of the first six seals, a general introduction to the seals: the seals signify something hidden from men, and loosing them means that God wanted to declare to us what was hidden from us, and the seals all point to events that will happen in the earthly world from the ascension of Christ into heaven until His coming, and the first four seals are concerned with these.. while the other three are scenes of heavenly matters that God also teaches us about.
